title: What if you boiled an egg on top of Everest?
caption:
Boiling water can't cook this egg on Everest. 🥚🏔️

At the summit the air pressure is about a third of sea level (253 vs 760 mmHg), so water boils at only about 70 °C instead of 100 °C.

Most of the egg white is ovalbumin, which needs about 80 °C to set. The yolk sets at roughly 62–70 °C, so the yolk can firm up while the white stays soft. That's why high-altitude cooks reach for a pressure cooker.

Send this to the friend who times their boiled eggs to the second.

Tomorrow: popcorn on Mars. 🔔 Follow @the.impossible.lab (or subscribe on YouTube) so you don't miss it.

⚠️ Don't try this. Undercooked eggs can carry Salmonella, and water at 70 °C still scalds.

sources: West JB et al. (1983) Barometric pressures at extreme altitudes on Mt. Everest, J Appl Physiol 54:1188-1194 (summit 253 Torr ≈ 1/3 of 760): https://air.unimi.it/bitstream/2434/176393/2/23-83JAP_Mount_Everest.pdf

CK-12 / LibreTexts Introductory Chemistry 13.9 Boiling: 'the boiling point on top of Mount Everest is only about 70°C' (8,848 m): https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Introductory_Chemistry/Introductory_Chemistry_(CK-12)/13:_States_of_Matter/13.09:_Boiling

IFLScience, 'This is why you can't boil an egg on Mount Everest': water boils at 68 °C with about one-third of sea-level pressure; ovalbumin (up to 54 % of the white) doesn't coagulate until 80 °C; yolk needs at least 70 °C; recommends a pressure cooker: https://www.iflscience.com/this-is-why-you-cant-boil-an-egg-on-mount-everest-74028

Modern Pastry and Plated Desserts (BCcampus open textbook), Coagulation: white coagulates 60–65 °C, yolk 62–70 °C; ovalbumin 54 %, ovotransferrin 12 % of white proteins: https://opentextbc.ca/modernpastryandplateddesserts/chapter/coagulation/
Computed check: Antoine equation for water at 253 mmHg → 71.9 °C (consistent with the 68–72 °C range); Everest height 8,848.86 m (2020 China–Nepal survey) → 8,849 m
